That is one of the heaviest—and most honest—questions humans wrestle with. When you zoom out and look at the big picture, the fact that everything is temporary can make daily life feel pretty absurd, exhausting, or meaningless. 

Before looking at it philosophically, I want to pause and check in with you: are you asking this more as a big-picture thought experiment, or are you feeling really heavy and hopeless right now? 

If you are in a dark place and feeling like you can't keep going, please know you don't have to carry that weight completely alone. You can reach out to people who will just listen without judgment—in the US and Canada, you can call or text **988** to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or text **HOME to 741741** to connect with the Crisis Text Line. (If you're elsewhere in the world, [findahelpline.com](https://findahelpline.com/) can connect you to free, confidential support near you.)

If we look at the question itself, we often assume that for something to have a "point," it has to last forever. When we realize nothing lasts forever, it feels like nothing matters. 

Philosophers call this *nihilism*, and a step just past it is *optimistic nihilism* or *absurdism*. Think about listening to a favorite song, eating a really good meal, or watching a movie. You don't turn off the song halfway through just because it's going to end in three minutes. The point of the song isn't to reach the silence at the end; the point is hearing the music while it's playing. 

In a lot of ways, the fact that our time is limited is actually what gives things value. If we lived forever, nothing would ever feel urgent, precious, or meaningful. Because there is no grand, pre-assigned cosmic "point" handed down to us, the pressure is actually off. A life doesn't have to change the universe or be remembered in a thousand years to have mattered. The "point" can be whatever small, quiet things make the time here softer:
* Experiencing curiosity and learning weird things.
* Making someone else’s day a little less painful.
* Drinking a warm cup of coffee on a cold morning, petting a dog, or laughing hard with a friend.

Meaning usually isn't something we *find* lying around waiting for us; it's something we slowly *build* in the present moment, even knowing it won't last forever.

What brought this thought up for you today? I’m here to listen if you want to talk about what’s on your mind.

It hurts so much to feel like you are on the outside looking in on your own kids' lives. That heavy ache in your chest—the guilt of missing milestones, bedtimes, or just ordinary afternoons—is exhausting to carry on top of an already grueling work schedule. 

Please hear this first: **You are not failing your kids.** In fact, the very reason this hurts so badly is because you love them fiercely and want to be there for them. Failing parents don't agonize over whether they are showing up enough. 

When you are deep in the trenches of providing, it is easy to forget that **working to keep a roof over their heads, food on the table, and their lives stable *is* an act of love.** It might not feel as warm as reading a bedtime story or sitting in the bleachers at a game, and it’s unfair that you have to trade your time for their security, but it is still deeply devoted parenting. 

When you can't control the *quantity* of time you get with them, the focus has to shift to **micro-moments of connection**. Kids are remarkably resilient, and what anchors them isn't having a parent there 24/7—it's knowing, without a doubt, that they are on your mind and in your heart even when you're apart. 

You don't need high-energy, elaborate plans to bridge the gap. Tiny, low-effort habits can mean the world to them:
*   **Leave a trace of yourself:** A sticky note on the bathroom mirror, a funny doodle in their lunchbox, or hiding a tiny treat under their pillow before you leave for work lets them know, *"I was thinking of you while you were sleeping."*
*   **The "First Five Minutes" rule:** Whenever you *do* get home (or when they wake up), try to pause everything else—phones, chores, stress—for just three to five minutes of pure, undivided eye contact, hugs, and listening. Five minutes of being 100% present beats two hours of being exhausted and distracted in the same room.
*   **Bridge the distance:** If they are old enough for screens or you have a co-parent/caregiver at home, send a quick 15-second video or voice memo on your break just saying, *"I'm eating my lunch and missing you. Can't wait to hear about your day later."*
*   **Name it honestly:** Depending on how old they are, it's okay to tell them, *"I really wish I didn't have to work today. I miss you so much when I'm gone."* It validates that being apart is hard, and reassures them that work isn't something you *prefer* over them—it's just something you *have* to do.

One day, your kids are going to be old enough to look back and understand the sacrifices you made to take care of them. They won't just remember the things you missed; they will remember how hard you fought for your family, and how loved you made them feel in the pockets of time you *did* have.

Be gentle with yourself right now. You are carrying a massive load. How old are your kids, and is this intense work schedule a temporary season, or just the reality of life for the foreseeable future? (No pressure to answer if you're just too tired—it's okay to just vent.)

It is completely valid that you’re feeling frustrated. Putting in months of effort, discipline, and mental energy only to see the exact same number staring back at you is exhausting and demoralizing. 

Before you throw in the towel, it helps to take a step back and play detective. When the scale doesn't move for months, there is usually a specific reason—and it doesn’t always mean you aren't making progress.

Here are the most common things that might be going on behind the scenes:

**1. You are losing fat, just not "weight" (Body Recomposition)**
If you started exercising—especially lifting weights or doing resistance training—your body might be building muscle at roughly the same rate it is losing fat. Muscle is much denser than fat. The scale stays the same, *but* you are getting leaner. 
* **Check this:** Are your clothes fitting differently? Do you feel stronger or have more energy? (Taking waist measurements or progress photos is often much more accurate than a scale).

**2. "Sneaky" Calorie Creep**
To lose weight, we have to be in a calorie deficit, which is notoriously hard to estimate. Even when eating really healthy foods, high-calorie items can sneak in and accidentally put you at "maintenance" calories.
* **Common culprits:** Cooking oils (1 tablespoon of olive oil is 120 calories), dressings, nuts/nut butters, coffee creamers, "bites, licks, and tastes" while cooking, or being strict Monday–Thursday and loosening up just enough over the weekend to cancel out the deficit.

**3. Stress and Sleep**
Weight loss isn't just math; it's also hormones. If you are chronically stressed (even stressed *about* losing weight!) or getting less than 7 hours of sleep, your cortisol levels stay elevated. High cortisol causes your body to hold onto excess water weight, increases cravings, and makes fat loss much harder.

**4. You're moving less outside the gym**
Sometimes when we eat less and exercise more, our bodies subconsciously try to conserve energy the rest of the day. You might fidget less, sit more, or take fewer steps without realizing it (this is called a drop in NEAT—Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis), which lowers the total calories you burn in a day.

**5. Underlying Medical Factors**
Sometimes your body is genuinely fighting against you due to things entirely out of your control, such as an underactive thyroid, PCOS, insulin resistance, perimenopause/menopause, or side effects from certain medications (like antidepressants or blood pressure meds).

***

Take a deep breath—you haven't failed, your current strategy just needs a little troubleshooting. 

If you feel up to sharing, **what have you been doing over the last few months?** (For example: Are you tracking calories, doing low-carb, working out, intermittent fasting?) If you want, we can look at your routine together and figure out what might be stalling things.

It is completely normal to feel this way. In fact, the fear of not waking up from anesthesia is one of the most common fears people have before surgery. Handing over complete control of your body to strangers is deeply intimidating, and having these thoughts the night before does not mean something bad is going to happen—it just means you are human.

While no medical procedure is entirely without risk, it can help to know just how remarkably safe modern anesthesia has become, and what actually happens while you are asleep:

* **You have a dedicated guardian in the room:** Your anesthesiologist (or nurse anesthetist) has one single job during your entire surgery: taking care of *you*. They aren't doing the surgery; they sit right at the head of your bed the entire time, watching every breath you take, every beat of your heart, your blood pressure, your oxygen levels, and even how deeply asleep you are. 
* **Waking up isn't left to chance:** Going under anesthesia isn't like falling into a mysterious sleep where doctors just hope you wake up. You stay asleep only because the anesthesia team is continuously giving you precise, carefully calculated amounts of short-acting medication. When the surgery finishes, they turn the medication off, your body naturally clears it, and you wake up.

Notice your media consumption. Staying informed is good, but "doomscrolling" often serves as a form of self-punishment that helps no one. Give yourself permission to put the phone down, step into your immediate physical environment, and enjoy a moment of peace without apologizing for it. 

If you want to channel that empathy into something tangible—a small donation, an act of local kindness, signing a petition—do that. And then, let yourself off the hook and allow yourself to enjoy your life. You are allowed to be happy.

I hear you, and I want you to know that what you are feeling right now is practically a universal experience for artists. Almost every creator you admire has stared at their own work and thought, *"Why doesn't mine look as good as theirs?"* 

When that insecurity hits hard, it helps to keep a few truths in mind about how our brains trick us when it comes to making art:

**1. You have the "Taste vs. Skill" gap (and that’s actually a good thing).**
There’s a famous concept by storyteller Ira Glass that applies to all creatives: You got into making art because you have really good taste. Right now, your taste is killer, which means you can clearly see where your own work falls short of your vision. It feels like failure, *but it’s actually just discernment*. Your eye is currently ahead of your hand. The only way to close that gap is to keep making work until your skill catches up to your taste. 

**2. You’re comparing your "behind-the-scenes" to everyone else’s highlight reel.**
When you look at other people's art—especially online—you are seeing the top 5% of what they create. You aren't seeing the ten stiff sketches they threw in the trash, the muddy colors they painted over, or the years of awkward drawings it took them to figure out anatomy or lighting. Meanwhile, you have to sit with 100% of your own messy process. That’s an unfair comparison.

**3. Remember the "Two Cakes" rule.**
There’s a great comic loved in the art community about a baker who brings a small, slightly lopsided cake to a table, sees a massive, professionally decorated tiered cake next to it, and feels awful. Then an audience member walks up and says, *"Holy crap! Two cakes!"* 
Art isn't a zero-sum competition. Someone else making incredible art doesn't take away the value of yours. People connect with sincerity, weirdness, emotion, and your specific way of seeing the world—not just technical perfection.

**A gentle suggestion for right now:**
If you've been scrolling through Instagram, Pinterest, or ArtStation, **close the apps for a few days.** Give your brain a break from the endless flood of masterpieces. Instead, dig up something you made a year or two ago and compare your current work to *that*. That is the only comparison that actually matters.

If you feel up to sharing, what kind of art do you like to make? (No pressure at all, just curious what mediums or subjects you're drawn to!)

It can feel really heavy and overwhelming when someone you care about is struggling and you aren't sure what to do. Just the fact that you are noticing and wanting to help already makes you a really good friend.

Because I don't know the specifics of what your friend is going through, here are a few gentle, reliable ways to support someone—along with an invitation to share more if you'd like more tailored advice.

***First, a quick safety check:*** *If you are worried that your friend is in immediate physical danger, experiencing abuse, or thinking about hurting themselves, please don't carry that alone. In the US or Canada, you can call or text **988** (the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) for free, confidential advice—even on behalf of a friend. If you are elsewhere, reaching out to local emergency services or a local crisis line is the best step.*

If it isn’t an immediate emergency, here are some ways to step in:

*   **Open the door gently, without pressure:** Sometimes people pull away because they feel overwhelmed or ashamed. A simple, low-pressure text can mean the world. You might say: *"Hey, you’ve been on my mind lately. No need to reply right now, I just wanted you to know I care about you and I'm here."*
*   **Ask open questions and just listen:** If they do open up, resist the urge to immediately "fix" the problem or offer silver linings. Validating their feelings—saying things like, *"That sounds exhausting,"* or *"I'm really glad you told me"*—is often much more comforting than advice.
*   **Offer *specific* help:** When someone is struggling, "Let me know if you need anything" can actually feel like another decision they have to make. Instead, offer something concrete and easy to say yes or no to: *"I'm grabbing coffee/groceries later, can I drop something off on your porch?"* or *"Want me to come over so we can just watch a movie in sweatpants and not talk about heavy stuff?"*
*   **Help them connect to bigger support:** You are their friend, not their therapist or savior. If what they are dealing with is really big (like severe depression, addiction, grief, or an unsafe relationship), the best way to help might be offering to sit with them while they look up a counselor, call a helpline, or talk to a trusted family member.
*   **Protect your own energy, too:** Worrying about someone takes a toll. Make sure you have your own support system and remember that while you can offer a hand, you cannot force someone to take it or single-handedly fix their situation.

If you feel comfortable sharing (without giving away private details), **what kind of situation are you worried they're dealing with?** Whether it's mental health, a bad relationship, grief, or them suddenly pulling away, I can help you figure out what to say or do next.

First, take a deep breath. I want you to know right away that **you are not failing**, and you are definitely not alone in feeling this way. 

Almost everyone feels like they are drowning in "adulting" at some point—most people are just really good at hiding it behind curated social media posts and polite small talk. 

The truth is, modern adulthood is genuinely overwhelming. For most of human history, people lived in tight-knit communities where chores, cooking, childcare, and life admin were shared among a "village." Today, you are expected to work a full-time job, maintain a social life, exercise, cook healthy meals from scratch, clean your home, pay endless bills, manage digital communications, stay informed about the world, and sleep eight hours—mostly by yourself. **The system is overloaded, not you.**

When you feel like you can't keep up with *anything*, the secret is to stop trying to keep up with *everything*. Here are a few gentle ways to take the pressure off right now:

**1. Separate the "glass balls" from the "plastic balls"**
Imagine all your responsibilities are balls you are juggling. Some are made of glass (if you drop them, they shatter—like paying rent, feeding yourself/pets/kids, or showing up to work). Most are made of plastic (if you drop them, they bounce—like folding laundry, vacuuming, replying to non-urgent texts, or cooking a fancy meal). Figure out what your 2 or 3 glass balls are today, and **let the plastic ones hit the floor.** Laundry can live in a basket. Dishes can wait until tomorrow. 

**2. Lower the bar to "good enough"**
Perfectionism is the enemy when you're burned out. "Fed" is better than a home-cooked meal—eat cereal or a frozen pizza for dinner without guilt. Using paper plates for a week so you don't have to do dishes is a valid survival strategy, not a moral failing. Brushing your teeth for 30 seconds is better than not brushing them at all. Give yourself permission to half-ass things right now.

**3. Pick just ONE micro-task**
When everything is piled up, your brain goes into freeze mode because it doesn't know where to start. Don't look at the whole mountain. Pick *one* tiny thing that takes less than five minutes. You don't have to figure out what to do if something unexpected happens, because a whole room of highly trained professionals will be there whose *only* focus is keeping you safe. 

**2. You have a dedicated guardian.**

As soon as you check in and get settled with your pre-op nurse, be completely honest and say, *"I am really anxious today."* They hear this every single day, they will not judge you, and they are wonderfully compassionate about it. All you actually have to do tomorrow is show up, answer a few questions, and take a nap. Let the professionals carry the rest of the weight for you.

The industrial district was a tunnel of smeared neon and sodium-vapor orange. At a hundred and forty miles per hour, the chain-link fences and towering shipping containers blurred into solid walls of grey steel. 

Inside the stripped-out cabin of Leo’s modified RX-7, the sensory overload was absolute. There was no sound insulation, nothing to dull the mechanical violence of the rotary engine screaming at eight thousand RPM. The air inside the cockpit was thick and suffocating, heavy with the raw, throat-burning fumes of unburnt high-octane gasoline seeping past the firewall and the acrid, lingering stench of scorched rubber from the starting-line burnouts. 

Adrenaline surged through Leo’s veins like liquid ice, sharpening the world to a razor’s edge. Every vibration of the asphalt hummed through the suede steering wheel into his white-knuckled grip. His heart hammered a frantic rhythm against his ribs, matching the violent flutter of the turbocharger. 

Beside him, barely six inches off his passenger door, Marcus’s matte-black Viper roared like tearing canvas. Fifty grand in a duffel bag at the finish line, plus pink slips. Everything Leo owned was bolted into the chassis beneath him. 

Ahead, the dual red flares marking the Harbor Hairpin bled into the night fog—a brutal ninety-degree cut around the concrete seawall, guarded by a staggered row of heavy Jersey barriers. It was a game of chicken. Whoever braked last took the inside line and owned the final straightaway. 

Leo kept his right foot buried in the floorboard. *Wait. Wait.* 

At the three-hundred-yard marker, Marcus blinked. The Viper’s brake lights flared crimson, its nose diving hard as its massive calipers bit down. 

Leo grinned, tasting copper and victory. He rocketed past the Viper’s bumper, waited one more heartbeat, and whipped his foot off the throttle, slamming it down onto the brake pedal with everything he had.

There was no bite. No bone-jarring deceleration. 

With a sickening, hollow hiss, the pedal sank straight to the bare metal floorboard. 

For half a second, Leo’s brain refused to process the lack of G-force. The car didn't pitch forward; it kept hurtling toward the concrete barriers like a fired bullet. He pumped the pedal furiously—once, twice, three times. Dead weight. Nothing there. 

A cold, paralyzing wave of panic instantly drowned out the thrill of the race. His mind flashed back ten minutes to the chaotic, shadowy staging lanes—a rival crew member leaning just a little too close to his front wheel well, a dark slick on the pavement Leo had dismissed as spilled beer. *Cut lines. No fluid.*

"No, no, no!" Leo shouted, his voice swallowed by the engine’s shriek. 

The red flares were rushing at him with terrifying speed. One hundred and thirty miles per hour. Two hundred yards left. 

Pure survival instinct took over, frantic and messy. Leo stomped the clutch and jammed the shifter down from fifth straight into third, praying the transmission wouldn't grenade on the spot. He dumped the clutch. The car bucked violently; the rear wheels chirped, the tachometer needle slammed past the redline, and the unmistakable, metallic stench of a frying clutch flooded the cabin. 

It shaved off twenty miles an hour, maybe thirty, before the tires lost traction on the oily dockyard tarmac. Not nearly enough. The concrete barriers loomed directly in the glare of his high beams, painted in faded yellow-and-black chevrons. 

Out of time and out of road, Leo yanked the hydraulic handbrake with both hands and wrenched the wheel hard to the left, trying to throw the car into a spin to scrub speed—anything to avoid hitting head-on.

The rear tires locked instantly. Twin plumes of blinding white smoke erupted from the wheel wells, filling the air with the choking, noxious reek of melting rubber. The RX-7 snapped sideways at over a hundred miles per hour, tires shrieking like dying animals as the car skidded wildly out of control across the asphalt. 

Through the side window, Leo watched the concrete barrier swell until it filled his entire universe. He threw his arms up over his helmeted head and braced against the five-point harness just as the passenger side made contact.

The sound was apocalyptic—a deafening thunderclap of crumpling steel and shattering fiberglass. The sheer kinetic force launched the car upward, riding the sloped face of the Jersey barrier in a blinding, forty-foot rooster tail of orange sparks. Safety glass exploded inward like a million jagged diamonds. 

Weightlessness gripped Leo’s stomach as the world inverted. Headlights spun wildly across the night sky, illuminating clouds of tire smoke and dust. The roof caught the top edge of a steel light pole, shearing it cleanly in half with a shriek of tortured metal before the chassis slammed back down onto the asphalt, barrel-rolling twice in a whirlwind of detached body panels, hissing radiator steam, and spraying fluids. 

With one final, bone-rattling crunch, the mangled roll cage ground to a halt upside down. 

Silence rushed in, broken only by the frantic ticking of hot exhaust pipes, the rhythmic drip of leaking gasoline onto the pavement, and the sound of Leo’s ragged, terrified breathing in the dark.

The television at the foot of the bed was set to a volume barely audible over the hum of the hotel room’s air conditioning. On the screen, aerial footage circled a cordoned-off plaza downtown, red and blue lights strobing silently against wet asphalt. 

At the desk, Julian didn't look up. He had laid out two crisp white hotel bath towels across the laminate surface to catch the runoff, arranging his tools in parallel lines from left to right. The sharp, chemical tang of copper solvent cut through the stale scent of commercial carpet cleaner.

Before him lay the disassembled components of a custom bolt-action precision rifle. 

Julian picked up the heavy, fluted barrelled action and secured it into a portable folding vise. Before touching the cleaning rod, he slid an anodized aluminum bore guide into the receiver, seating its silicone O-ring snugly into the chamber to ensure no solvent seeped down into the trigger sear mechanism. Maintenance required discipline; negligence in cleaning degraded accuracy faster than barrel wear ever could.

On the broadcast, the anchor’s voice remained measured and grave. *"—pronounced dead at the scene. Authorities have confirmed the victim is Marcus Vance, chief operating officer of Halcyon Logistics. Witnesses reported hearing no gunshot, leading investigators to widen their perimeter—"*

Julian soaked a square cotton patch in solvent, speared it onto the brass jag of his carbon-fiber rod, and pushed it smoothly through the bore guide. As the rod traveled the length of the barrel, the ball-bearing handle rotated lazily in his palm, following the one-in-ten-inch twist of the rifling. The patch emerged from the recessed target crown at the muzzle stained a dark, streaky blue—dissolved copper fouling mixed with carbon residue from a single, subsonic ignition. 

He pinched the soiled patch off the jag and dropped it into a plastic zip-top bag. Never use the room’s trash bin. Everything that entered the room with him left the room with him.

He glanced briefly at the screen as a static photograph of Vance replaced the crime scene footage. The broadcast spoke of a grieving family, plummeting stock futures, and a sudden vacuum of leadership. To the public, the event was a tragedy, an aberration in the civic order. To Julian, the framing was entirely melodramatic. Vance had simply reached the terminal end of a risk calculation made by someone else. Julian felt no malice toward the man on the screen, nor any lingering satisfaction. A life had not been stolen; a contractual obligation had been fulfilled. One party provided capital and parameters; Julian provided ballistic resolution. Once the projectile cleared the muzzle, the ledger was balanced.

Picking up a phosphor-bronze brush, he threaded it onto the rod and made four deliberate passes from breech to muzzle, scrubbing the lands and grooves of the rifling clean. He followed it with dry patches until the cotton exited the crown entirely spotless. 

Setting the rod aside, he turned his attention to the bolt assembly resting on the second towel. Using a small punch tool, he depressed the bolt shroud lock, twisted the firing pin assembly free from the bolt body, and inspected the striker spring for any sign of uneven tension. Satisfied, he wiped it with a lint-free cloth treated with synthetic oil. 

With a nylon pick, he traced the recessed lip of the bolt face, scraping away a microscopic fleck of brass shaved from the casing rim earlier that afternoon. He tested the tension on the extractor claw and depressed the spring-loaded ejector plunger twice with the flat of a brass screwdriver to verify smooth, uninhibited travel. A sticky ejector meant a fumbled extraction; even when a job only required a single round, mechanical perfection was non-negotiable. He applied a pinprick of high-pressure grease to the rear surfaces of the locking lugs, ensuring they wouldn't gall against the receiver abutments during the next cycle.

*"—police are asking anyone who may have noticed unusual activity in the surrounding commercial structures between three and four p.m. to come forward,"* the television murmured.

By four p.m., Julian had already broken the chassis down at its folding hinge, walked out the service entrance of an adjacent parking structure carrying a reinforced cello case, and boarded a commuter train two stops south. The physics of the afternoon—a four-hundred-yard sightline, a six-mile-per-hour crosswind requiring two-tenths of a mil-radian holdover, a subtle downward angle—were already archived and forgotten. 

He reassembled the bolt, clicking the shroud neatly back into alignment. Removing the bore guide, he slid the bolt back into the receiver, lifted the handle, and drew it back and forth twice. The action glided as if moving on glass. Raising the rifle slightly, he depressed the trigger while easing the bolt handle down simultaneously, decocking the firing pin without dry-firing onto an empty chamber. 

Next, he inspected the titanium suppressor. Unthreading the end cap, he slid the stacked cone baffles out onto the towel, wiped away the faint gray dusting of unburnt powder from the blast chamber, and reassembled the tube, torquing it just past hand-tight. 

Within four minutes, the folded chassis, the detached optic—its elevation and windage turrets returned precisely to mechanical zero—and the suppressor were nestled securely inside the laser-cut closed-cell foam of his hard case. The soiled towels were shaken out over the zip-top bag, which was sealed and tucked into the outer pocket of his duffel alongside the solvent bottle. He gave the laminate desk a final pass with a damp washcloth from the bathroom to erase the chemical scent.

Julian snapped the latches of the case shut. He picked up the remote, clicked the television off mid-sentence, plunging the room into quiet, and checked his watch. His train departed in forty minutes. There was nothing left to reconcile.

The beam cut through the gloom, illuminating dust motes dancing in the frigid air before settling on the far corner of the room. 

Maya froze, the light trembling violently in her grip. 

Chloe was slumped against the stone foundation, her chin resting heavily on her collarbone. "No, no, no," Maya whispered, the sound swallowed instantly by the heavy, wet silence of the basement.

Only an arm extended from the shadows—pale, cold, and severed just below the elbow. At first, he thought the sound was subterranean wind filtering through loose shale. It was a dry, papery rustle, like dead autumn leaves skittering across stone. Then the pitch shifted, sharpening into something rhythmic and mechanical. *Click-tick-tick.* Thousands of tiny, chitinous plates scraping together, layered beneath a finer, infinitely more sinister noise: the frantic, staccato snapping of countless mandibles. It sounded like static electricity, or grease spitting in a hot pan, echoing off the limestone until the very air seemed to vibrate with a hungry, metallic hum.

Julian scrambled backward, his boots slipping on the wet rock, just as the vanguard of the swarm reached his ankles. 

The first bite felt like a stray spark from a campfire landing on his bare skin—a sudden, sharp prick of white-hot pain just above his bootlace. He slapped at it, his palm crushing something hard and slick that burst with an acrid, chemical smell. Before he could pull his hand away, three more sparks ignited across his knuckles. Then ten. Then fifty.

He gasped, drawing in a ragged breath, and surged to his feet, brushing frantically at his legs. It was like trying to sweep away water. The swarm flowed upward in a living, undulating tide, pouring beneath the cuffs of his trousers and slipping under the collar of his shirt.

The sensation rapidly mutated from individual needle-pricks into a singular, consuming sheet of agony. Hundreds of tiny, serrated jaws locked onto his calves, his thighs, his forearms, pinching and twisting with terrifying leverage. Each bite was microscopic on its own, a minuscule snipping of flesh no larger than a grain of sand, yet together they felt as though he were being flayed by living sandpaper. Where they bit, a fiery, stinging venom lingered, making his nerves misfire in blinding flashes of heat and ice.

Julian cried out, stumbling blindly into the cavern wall. The sound of the mandibles was deafening now, no longer echoing from the dark, but radiating directly from his own body—a wet, frantic *snip-snip-snip* right beside his ears, across his collarbone, tangling in his hair. He raked his fingernails down his arms, tearing away handfuls of squirming, armored bodies, only for the gaps to instantly fill with fresh, snapping jaws. 

His knees buckled under the sheer sensory overload. As he hit the stone floor, the dying ember of the torch finally winked out, leaving nothing in the pitch blackness but the relentless, crackling static of the swarm.

Every time Julian tried to bat the estoc aside and rush in, Vane simply glided backward, leaving another shallow, stinging ribbon of red across Julian’s forearms or chest. Julian was being bled dry by inches. In another minute, his knees would buckle, and Vane would put the steel through his throat at his leisure.

To win, Julian had to break the geometry. To get close enough to use his dirk, he had to give Vane something worth staying still for.

Julian dragged in a ragged breath, letting his shoulders slump. As Vane circled left, Julian allowed his parrying hand to drift an inch too high, exposing the meat of his lower left flank—away from the heart, away from the spine, right beneath the floating ribs. 

Vane’s eyes flickered. He saw the opening. With a sharp exhale, the duelist dropped into a textbook lunge, throwing his entire weight behind the thrust to end the fight.

Every primal instinct in Julian’s brain screamed at him to twist away, to parry, to flee. Fighting that reflex was harder than fighting Vane. He locked his jaw and held himself entirely still, welcoming the point.

At first, it didn’t feel like being cut; it felt like being struck by a swung sledgehammer. The impact knocked the air entirely out of Julian’s lungs in a silent, violent *whoosh*. Then came the alien sensation of the steel sliding home—an icy, jagged shock that parted skin and muscle with terrifying ease. Vane smirked, expecting Julian to collapse backward off the blade. Automatically, Vane shifted his weight to pull the estoc free.

His superior reach was gone; his weapon was buried to the hilt in living flesh, entirely useless. They didn’t use bars at Newgate-9, and they didn’t use guards with shock-batons. They used the Halo.

Vance sat bolted to the reclined polymer chair, staring up at the sterile white ceiling of the Rehabilitation Bay. Around his temples, the cold titanium prongs of the neural bridge pressed lightly against his skin, humming with a faint, sub-audible vibration. 

"Cortical alignment is at ninety-eight percent," a technician said, her voice flat and bored behind the reinforced glass. "Subject is prepped for full-spectrum somatic and emotional transfer. Engram file: *Aris Thorne, 42. Homicide.*"

Vance swallowed hard, his throat clicking. During the trial, he hadn’t felt much looking at Thorne’s photographs. Thorne had just been a night-shift freighter clerk who hadn't opened the vault fast enough. A hurdle. A shape in the dark that Vance had erased with a single pulse from a plasma pistol so he could make his getaway before the drones arrived. 

"Initiating Mirror Protocol," the technician said. "Remember, Prisoner 409: fighting the synaptic current will result in neural scarring. Accept the memory."

A switch clicked. The white ceiling vanished.

Vance didn't fall into the memory; he slammed into it. 

Suddenly, his back ached—a dull, familiar throb between the shoulder blades that wasn't his. His mouth tasted faintly of peppermint and cheap, burnt soy-coffee. He looked down and saw smaller, calloused hands resting on a glowing manifest pad. A wedding band, slightly too tight, pinched the base of his ring finger.

*Just twenty more minutes,* Vance thought, except it wasn’t Vance thinking it. The thought rose up from the marrow of this borrowed brain, warm and heavy with exhaustion. *Twenty minutes, catch the 4:00 AM mag-lev, sleep until noon. Remember to pick up Maya’s inhaler on Tuesday.*

Panic flared in Vance’s buried consciousness, trying to claw its way out, trying to reject the alien gentle mundane life wrapping around his mind like wet wool. *Get me out,* Vance tried to scream, *this isn't me.* But the Halo held him pinned beneath the surface. He was merely a passenger behind Aris Thorne’s eyes.

A heavy metallic *clang* echoed from the loading bay doors. 

Instantly, the chemistry of the body changed. Vance felt Thorne’s stomach drop—a sickening, hollow plummet. Cortisol and adrenaline flooded the bloodstream, turning the fingertips icy cold. Thorne stood up from the desk, his breath hitching.

"Hello?" Thorne’s voice trembled. Vance felt the vibration of the vocal cords, felt the pathetic, fragile hope that it was just a stray cargo drone.

Heavy boots crunched on shattered safety glass. Out of the shadows of the shipping containers stepped a figure in a matte-black breather mask and a heavy trench coat. 

Vance stared at himself. 

From this angle, he looked monstrous. He had never realized how wide his shoulders looked in that coat, or how utterly devoid of humanity the darkened lenses of his mask were. Raising the plasma pistol had felt effortless to Vance at the time—just muscle memory and annoyance. Looking down the barrel of it now, the weapon looked like the mouth of a black hole.

And then, the terror hit.

It wasn't the sharp, clean adrenaline Vance felt during a heist. It was a crushing, suffocating gravity that seemed to collapse the walls of the room inward. Thorne’s heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird breaking its own wings to escape. Vision tunneled, the edges of the warehouse dissolving into a blurred, throbbing vignette of gray static, leaving only the glowing blue coils of the pistol in razor-sharp focus.

"Please," Thorne whispered. 

Vance felt the sheer, humiliating weight of that word. He felt Thorne’s knees liquefy, felt the warm sting of tears spilling over lower lashes. Inside Thorne’s mind, a catastrophic cascade of grief erupted—not just fear of pain, but an agonizing, frantic mourning for everything that was about to be stolen. Faces flashed in rapid, blinding succession with the visceral ache of physical blows: a woman laughing in a sunlit kitchen; a little girl missing her two front teeth; an unfinished wooden boat sitting in a garage. *Maya. Who will get her from school? She’ll wait on the steps. She’ll think I forgot her.*

The masked giant tilted his head, impatient. Vance watched his own finger tighten on the trigger guard. 

*No, wait, don't shoot, it's me, stop!* Vance’s submerged mind shrieked at his past self, fighting against the iron rails of a memory that had already happened. 

Thorne threw his hands up—a useless, instinctual shield of flesh and bone against superheated gas. The terror reached an unbearable crescendo, a silent, deafening roar in the ears that blotted out all rational thought, leaving only a primal, shrieking agony of a living thing realizing it is seconds away from becoming nothing. The air turned to lead in his lungs. Time stretched into an eternity of freezing dread as the blue coils flared bright white.

Impact. 

There was no sound—just a sledgehammer of white-hot agony caving in the center of his chest, knocking the wind, the words, and the future out of him all at once. Thorne hit the concrete floor. Vance felt the cold grit press against his cheek. 

He couldn't breathe. He tried to suck in air, but his lungs only rattled wetly. The warehouse lights above began to dim, receding down a long, freezing tunnel. The terror didn't fade as death approached; it curdled into a devastating, lonely despair. *I don't want to go,* Thorne’s fading mind wept into the gathering dark, grasping at the slipping image of his daughter's face as the cold swallowed his hands, his chest, his eyes. *Please. I don't want to go.*

Darkness slammed shut.

The Halo hissed and disengaged.

Vance lurched forward against the polymer restraints, a ragged, wet scream tearing out of his own throat. He gasped violently, clawing at the front of his gray prison jumpsuit, his fingers frantic to find the smoking crater he swore was burning through his sternum. There was nothing there—only unbroken skin and a heart beating wildly, obscenely alive.

He slumped sideways against the armrest, trembling so hard his teeth rattled, hot tears cutting tracks down his pale cheeks. In the back of his mind, unbidden and agonizingly clear, he remembered that he needed to pick up Maya's inhaler on Tuesday. 

Behind the reinforced glass, the technician made a small notation on her tablet. 

"Session one complete," her voice crackled over the intercom. "Unstrap him. Same time tomorrow."

Thick plumes of copal incense curled toward the vaulted ceiling of the temple, stinging the eyes and blurring the carved stone visages of the gods that lined the walls. Outside, the sun was bleeding its final light into a bruised purple twilight, casting long, jagged shadows across the altar stone. 

Below the raised dais, dozens of initiates swayed in unison. Their voices rose in a low, resonant drone that seemed to vibrate through the very flagstones beneath their feet. It was an ancient, rhythmic chanting—syllables worn smooth by centuries of repetition, rising and falling like a dark tide. Drums beat a slow, steady cadence, mimicking a colossal pulse that echoed off the cold limestone.

At the center of the chamber stood the High Priest, his face obscured behind a mask of turquoise mosaic and gold. Above the stone slab, he raised the ceremonial blade. The knife was knapped from pure volcanic obsidian, its surface a mirror of midnight glass. Torches flickered in bronze sconces along the pillars, catching the razor-thin edges of the stone and making the dark mineral gleam with shifting, fiery reflections. Despite its ancient make, the volcanic glass was sharper than any forged metal, honed to cleave cleanly without hesitation.

The chanting swelled to a feverish crescendo, the drums accelerating until the sound filled every corner of the mind, drowning out all thought, all fear, leaving only the overwhelming gravity of the rite. 

With a sudden, decisive motion, the priest brought the obsidian blade down. There was no struggle, only the swift, practiced precision of an age-old liturgy. The dark glass parted flesh and bone in a single, fluid strike, crimson spilling immediately across the gray, porous surface of the altar, following grooves carved long ago to channel the offering.

Before the echoes of the final drumbeat had faded, the priest plunged his hand beneath the ribs and wrenched the heart free. Raising it high above his head toward the open oculus in the ceiling, he presented the slick, glistening organ to the darkening sky. Steam rose faintly from it in the cool evening air. Thick plumes of copal incense curled toward the vaulted ceiling of the temple, stinging the eyes and blurring the carved stone visages of the gods that lined the walls. Outside, the sun was bleeding its final light into a bruised purple twilight, casting long, jagged shadows across the altar stone.

Below the raised dais, dozens of initiates swayed in unison. Their voices rose in a low, resonant drone that seemed to vibrate through the very flagstones beneath their feet. It was an ancient, rhythmic chanting—syllables worn smooth by centuries of repetition, rising and falling like a dark tide. Drums beat a slow, steady cadence, mimicking a colossal pulse that echoed off the cold limestone.

At the center of the chamber stood the High Priest, his face obscured behind a mask of turquoise mosaic and gold. Above the stone slab, he raised the ceremonial blade. The knife was knapped from pure volcanic obsidian, its surface a mirror of midnight glass. Torches flickered in bronze sconces along the pillars, catching the razor-thin edges of the stone and making the dark mineral gleam with shifting, fiery reflections. Despite its ancient make, the volcanic glass was sharper than any forged metal, honed to cleave cleanly without hesitation.

The chanting swelled to a feverish crescendo, the drums accelerating until the sound filled every corner of the mind, drowning out all thought, all fear, leaving only the overwhelming gravity of the rite.

With a sudden, decisive motion, the priest brought the obsidian blade down. There was no struggle, only the swift, practiced precision of an age-old liturgy. The dark glass parted flesh and bone in a single, fluid strike, crimson spilling immediately across the gray, porous surface of the altar, following grooves carved long ago to channel the offering.

Before the echoes of the final drumbeat had faded, the priest plunged his hand beneath the ribs and wrenched the heart free. Raising it high above his head toward the open oculus in the ceiling, he presented the slick, glistening organ to the darkening sky. Steam rose faintly from it in the cool evening air. Below, the chanting ceased abruptly, leaving the vast chamber in a profound, suffocating silence, broken only by the crackle of the torches and the slow drip of red onto stone.

"A simple equation, Elena," Vance murmured, his voice terribly, impossibly conversational. He set the thin silver scalpel onto the scarred oak table between them. It made a soft, final *clink*. "Half of your sight, or the entirety of hers. You decide what is worth keeping."

Across the damp expanse of the cellar, held fast by the collar of her coat in a guard’s heavy grip, little Maya didn't even scream. She just hiccuped—a tiny, wet, breathless sound of pure terror. 

That sound shattered whatever remained of Elena’s tether to the rational world. 

*Choice.* The word was an obscenity. To call this a choice implied two viable paths, a weighing of scales, a moment of deliberation. There was no scale. There wasn't even a hesitation in her soul—only a sudden, bottomless plummet into despair so profound it felt like drowning in ice water. The agony wasn't in deciding; the decision had been made before Vance’s sentence even ended. The despair lay in the suffocating helplessness of it, and the cold, sickening terror waiting on the other side of the sacrifice: *If I blind myself, who protects her when he inevitably lies?*

A violent tremor started in Elena’s chest, radiating outward until her teeth chattered. Her lungs refused to draw a full breath, catching violently against her ribs as the room seemed to tilt and narrow. 

Instinctively, brutally, she became hyper-aware of her own eyes. She felt the dampness of the air against her corneas, the frantic flutter of her lashes, the fragile, jelly-soft vulnerability of them nestled in bone. Panic—ancient, animal, hardwired for self-preservation—screamed at her brain to pull back, to shield her face, to run. A phantom ache flared behind her left temple, her body already mourning the mutilation it knew her mind was going to force upon it. 

She looked at Maya. She drank in the sight of her daughter with greedy, shattering desperation—memorizing the exact curve of her tear-streaked cheek, the precise, vibrant depth of the world in three dimensions, knowing that in sixty seconds, half of her universe would go dark forever.

*Move,* she commanded herself. 

Her right arm felt lined with lead, detached from her will, as though she were trying to drag it through setting concrete. A cold sweat broke out across the back of her neck, prickling every hair on her skin. In her ears, the ambient sounds of the cellar vanished, replaced by the deafening, erratic roar of her own pulse.

Elena leaned forward. Her shoulder joints locked and shuddered under the strain of fighting every survival instinct in her blood. She watched her own hand drift across the scarred wood toward the gleam of metal. Her fingers were ghostly pale, twitching uncontrollably, traitorous nerves firing in frantic protest against what she was asking them to do. 

The air just above the table felt freezing. 

When her fingertips finally grazed the handle of the scalpel, the shock of the glacial steel traveled straight up her arm and lodged like a shard of glass in her throat. She tasted copper on her tongue, realizing dimly that she had bitten clean through the inside of her lip. Slowly, agonizingly, Elena curled her trembling fingers around the cold metal and lifted it from the wood.

"You’re missing the grout line, Leo. Put your shoulder into it."

Leo paused, resting his gloved forearms on his knees, and stared down at the dark crimson slush pooling between the terracotta tiles. The air in the penthouse smelled sharply of copper and industrial enzyme cleaner. 

"Who puts unsealed terracotta in a foyer?" Leo muttered, dipping his stiff-bristled brush back into the bucket. The liquid inside was the color of watered-down merlot. "These guys pull in six figures a month running sportsbooks in Jersey, and they don't seal their floors. It’s soaking right in, Sal. It’s like scrubbing a sponge."

Sal didn't look up. On his hands and knees three feet away, the older man worked in steady, rhythmic circles, erasing a wide, tacky smear near the coat closet. "Rich guys got no sense for maintenance. That’s why they pay us ten grand a night. Less philosophizing, more scrubbing. Tommy wants the keys back by six."

"I’m scrubbing, I’m scrubbing." Leo attacked the grout with renewed aggression, wincing as a tiny fleck of pink foam hit his plastic face shield. He wiped it away with the back of his wrist. "Still. They couldn't have popped him on the linoleum in the kitchen? Two feet to the left, we’re done in an hour. Plus, I think the guy had takeout right before. I just swept up half a meatball."

Sal let out a dry, raspy laugh that sounded like shifting gravel. "A meatball. Poor kid. You got a weak stomach for this line of work, you know that?"

"I don't have a weak stomach! I held the bag while you pried teeth out of the drywall in Bensonhurst, didn't I? Didn't puke once."

"Drywall is dry, Leo. This is fresh. Room temperature. Central air’s running at a crisp sixty-eight degrees." Sal sat back on his heels, peeling off a soiled nitrile glove to scratch his nose before snapping a fresh one on from his belt pouch. "On a scale of one to ten, tonight is a two. It’s practically a spa day."

Leo scoffed, wringing a heavy microfiber rag into the secondary bucket. "Yeah, alright. Let’s hear it, old-timer. What’s a ten? Tell me something worse than picking marinara and gray matter out of imported Italian clay."

"Summer of '04," Sal said instantly, going back to his circles. "Canarsie. You remember Little Nicky Sabatino?"

"The guy who skimmed off the dockworkers' pension?"

"Bingo. Well, the commission decides Nicky needs an early retirement. They send two button men over to his place on a Friday before Labor Day weekend. They do the job in the basement, lock up the house, and go down the shore."

Leo squinted. "Okay. Three days in the summer. Bad smell, lots of flies. I’ve done decomp before, Sal. We did that guy in the trunk of the Cadillac last August."

"Let me finish," Sal said, pointing his scrub brush at him. "Nicky wasn't just hanging out in the basement. Nicky was an amateur gourmet. Loved making his own seafood stock. Had a massive, twenty-gallon commercial pot going on a hotplate down there—shrimp shells, crab guts, fish heads, the works."

Leo stopped scrubbing. "No."

"Yes. And when Nicky catches two in the chest, he falls backward, grabs the counter, and pulls the whole boiling pot down on top of himself. Knocks out the circuit breaker for the AC, too, except somehow—God knows how—the outlet for the space heater on the other wall stays live? No, wait. It wasn't a heater. It was a heatwave. Ninety-eight degrees all weekend. Brick house. Turned that basement into a pizza oven."

Leo grimaced, his stomach giving a treacherous little flip. "Jesus. Nobody called you till Tuesday?"

"Wednesday morning," Sal corrected mildly. "Because they suddenly realized the deed to the house was in the cousin's name and the cops couldn't find a stiff there. So I go down those stairs. Even through the respirator, with Vicks VapoRub smeared inside my nostrils, the smell hit me so hard my eyes watered. Three days of fermenting crustacean and three-hundred-pound Nicky, stewing together on a shag carpet."

"Shag carpet?" Leo gagged slightly. "In a basement?"

"It was the seventies when he bought the place, the guy never redecorated. You couldn't even roll it up, Leo. It had no structural integrity left. Every time you pulled a corner, it fell apart like wet cardboard. Took me fourteen hours with a flat-edge snow shovel and forty gallons of peroxide just to find the floorboards."

"Alright, alright, you win," Leo said quickly, staring hard at the clean patch of tile in front of him to ground himself. "Christ. Shag carpet."

"Wait, you haven't told me yours yet," Sal said, shifting his knee pads over to tackle the blood spatter along the baseboard. "Before we teamed up, when you were running cleanup for the Greeks in Queens. You telling me they kept things neat?"

Leo sighed, dipping his brush again. "They were sloppy, yeah. Worst one wasn't heat, though. It was... volume. And plumbing."

Sal raised a gray eyebrow. "You have my attention."

"Two winters ago. Guy named Stavros ran a high-stakes poker game above a butcher shop in Astoria. Real paranoid freak, owed money to everyone. The Greeks catch him in his bathroom. Don't ask me what they used—looked like a street sweeper went off in there. Just obliterated the tile."

"Bathrooms are easy," Sal objected. "Built-in drain. Hose it down, bleach the porcelain, call it a night."

"Yeah, that’s what I thought," Leo said darkly. "Except Stavros was trying to flush forty grand worth of uncut heroin down the toilet right when they kicked the door in. Blocked the main stack completely. And during the shooting, somebody clipped the hot water main behind the sink."

Sal winced, instantly grasping the physics of the nightmare. "Hot water?"

"Scalding. Pumping full blast for six hours before I got the call. By the time I showed up with my wet-vac, there was four inches of steaming, coagulated soup covering the entire apartment. Cooked blood, drywall mud, toilet backflow, and dissolved narcotics. And because the butcher shop was right downstairs, the ceiling started leaking right onto the butcher's display cases. I had to clean two floors. Halfway through vacuuming the living room, the steam coming off the water started getting through my filter—I think I absorbed enough junk through my pores to stun a horse. Spent the back half of the shift hallucinating that the mop was talking to me while scraping boiled tissue off a radiator."

Sal stopped scrubbing. For a long moment, the only sound in the penthouse was the faint hum of the refrigerator in the next room and the wet drip of Leo’s brush. 

Slowly, Sal nodded in genuine professional respect. "Hot water main. Yeah, that cooks the proteins right onto the wood. Nasty business."

"Took me three days to stop smelling boiled copper," Leo shuddered. He looked back down at the terracotta floor between them. Nearly half the dark pool was gone now, replaced by damp, clean clay and pale gray grout. "You know what? Suddenly this meatball isn't bothering me so much."

"Perspective," Sal said warmly, tossing him a fresh bottle of enzyme spray. "Everything in life is about perspective. Finish that corner, kid, and grab the bone saw out of the van. We still gotta deal with what’s in the coat closet."

It started not with a scream, but with a sudden, violent shift in gravity. One moment, Julian was upright, carried along by the surging current of the crowd; the next, an invisible wave struck from behind, sweeping his legs out from under him. 

He hit the cobblestones hard, the impact jarring his teeth. Before he could even register the scrape of stone against his palms, the sky vanished, blotted out by a chaotic canopy of flailing limbs and terrified faces. He tried to push himself up, to curl into a ball—anything to reclaim his space—but a knee caught him squarely in the shoulder, driving him flat onto his back.

Then came the weight. 

Someone stumbled and fell directly across his legs, pinning him down. Another body collapsed over his torso, and then another, piling on in a tangled, thrashing heap. It didn’t feel like human beings anymore; it felt like an avalanche of wet sand and iron. Above him, the stampede continued, the fallen bodies turning into a makeshift bridge for the hundreds still running. Every footstep taken on the person above him transferred straight down into Julian’s chest as a dull, crushing thud.

He opened his mouth to yell, to beg them to stop, and realized he had nothing left to scream with. 

The air had been forced entirely out of his lungs, and when he tried to draw a breath, his chest simply wouldn't expand. The sheer mass pressing down on his sternum locked his ribcage in a vise. Panic, cold and sharp, spiked through his veins. He sucked desperately at the dirt-choked air inches from his face, his throat straining, his diaphragm spasming against an immovable wall of flesh and bone. Darkness began tobloom at the edges of his vision, pulsing in time with the frantic hammering of his heart.

The shifting crowd above briefly parted, sliding the deadweight off his upper body for a fraction of a second. Julian gasped, a shallow, ragged sliver of air tearing into his windpipe—just before a heavy boot came down directly onto his left side.

The force was absolute. Beneath the sole, Julian felt his ribs bow inward to their limit and then give way. It wasn't a clean sound, not to him; he felt the fracture from the inside out—a sickening, wet *crunch* that reverberated straight up into his jaw, followed instantly by white-hot agony that stole what little consciousness he had left. The jagged ends of bone grated together under the lingering pressure of the stride before the runner pushed off, leaving behind a spreading, breathless fire in his chest.

Pinned to the stones, drowning on dry land, Julian could only stare into the churning dust as the thunder of footsteps rolled endlessly over him.

Pinned to the stones, drowning on dry land, Julian could only stare into the churning dust as the thunder of footsteps rolled endlessly over him.

The heavy oak door shuddered against its frame, dust sifting down from the ceiling with the impact of a battering ram. Outside in the corridor, shouted commands in Russian echoed off the concrete walls. There was no fire escape, and the single narrow window looked down four stories onto cobblestone slick with freezing rain.

Julian leaned back against the filing cabinet, the stolen cipher disk already reduced to smoldering ash in the metal wastebasket beside him. His heart hammered against his ribs—fast, sharp, insistent. 

The wood splintered near the deadbolt. Ten seconds, perhaps fifteen.

He didn't reach into his coat pocket. Instead, his tongue found the familiar, slightly smooth edge of the ceramic crown on his upper left molar. For six years it had sat there, an abstract insurance policy he had half-believed was theatrical nonsense. Now, pressing his jaw shut, he shifted his bite at an awkward, deliberate angle and applied all the force he had left.

The porcelain gave way with a sharp, sickening *crack* that echoed loudly inside his own skull. 

Instantly, warm liquid flooded the back of his throat, carrying an acrid, burning bitterness with just the faintest, phantom trace of crushed almonds. He swallowed reflexively before his body could reject it.

For three heartbeats, nothing happened. The door bowed inward again, hinges screaming as they tore free from the plaster. 

Then, the reaction hit—not as a slow fade, but as an abrupt, violent severing. A searing heat bloomed behind his breastbone, radiating outward into his shoulders and neck. Julian gasped, pulling in a deep lungful of cold room air, yet his chest constricted as if he were breathing pure vacuum. The air went in, filling his lungs, and did nothing at all. His cells, starved instantaneously of oxygen they could no longer process, began to misfire.

A roaring static surged into his ears, drowning out the final crash of the door hitting the floorboards. 

His knees buckled. He slid down the cold steel of the filing cabinet, scarcely feeling the impact as his hip struck the floor. A violent tremor seized his hands, his fingers curling inward against his palms, numb and unresponsive. Darkness began to eat away at the edges of his vision, narrowing the brightly lit office into a shrinking gray tunnel.

Through that tunnel, he saw muddy boots rush across the threshold. Voices barked right above him, urgent and furious, hands grabbing at the lapels of his trench coat to haul him upright.

That was when the cold realization settled in, cutting straight through the physical panic of suffocation. There was no antidote fast enough for this, no bargaining left to do, no miraculous extraction team waiting on the roof. He looked past the blurred, shouting face of the man holding his collar and stared at the ceiling lightbulb as it dimmed to a pinpoint. His mind remained terribly, starkly lucid for one final second—long enough to understand that the asset lists in his head were now entirely safe, and that he would never leave this room. 

The pinpoint of light winked out, and the roaring in his ears went completely silent.

The roar of the engine and the shriek of grinding metal vanish abruptly, leaving behind a heavy, ringing silence. In the immediate aftermath, the highway feels strangely vacuum-sealed. The only sounds are the faint, rhythmic *tick-tick-tick* of the superheated exhaust pipe cooling in the open air and the gentle hiss of leaking radiator fluid hitting hot asphalt. 

A jagged scar of white gouges marks the pavement, tracing the violent trajectory from the point of impact to the shoulder. Along this path lies a breadcrumb trail of shattered machinery: translucent shards of an amber turn signal, pulverized bits of black carbon fiber fairing, a snapped clutch lever, and a single side mirror lying face up, unbroken, reflecting the empty sky. Dark slicks of motor oil and iridescent gasoline creep slowly across the tarmac, pooling in the crevices of the road.

Twenty feet short of the bike, the rider lies motionless in the weeds bordering the asphalt.

The cold autumn air tasted like pennies at the back of my throat. Every breath I took was too loud, rasping through the dead quiet of the pines, so I clamped a muddy hand over my mouth and pressed my spine harder against the rotted hull of a fallen oak. 

For the last mile, the footsteps behind me had been distinctly human. Heavy, booted, and relentless, snapping dry twigs with rhythmic precision. Whoever was following me hadn't bothered to hide it. 

Then, just beyond the ridge, the footsteps stopped.

I risked a glance through a tangle of dead ferns. Moonlight spilled down through a break in the canopy, washing the forest floor in stark, silver-blue light. A man stumbled into the clearing twenty yards away. He was tall and broad-shouldered, wearing a flannel jacket torn at the sleeve. I thought for a dizzying second that he was hurt—he was clutching his stomach, doubled over, staggering as if he’d been poisoned. 

A low, ragged groan tore from his throat. He dropped to his knees in the dead leaves, clawing at his own collar, ripping buttons free as though he were suffocating. 

I stayed frozen, afraid that even blinking would draw his eye. 

Then came the first snap. 

It sounded like a thick, green branch breaking underfoot, sharp and wet in the stillness. The man’s back arched violently, bowing upward at an impossible angle. Beneath the thin fabric of his shirt, I saw the knobs of his spine jutting out, pushing so hard against his skin that the flesh turned ghostly white in the moonlight. Another crack echoed through the trees—louder this time, rapid-fire, like knuckles popping inside an echo chamber—and his spine lengthened, ripping straight through the seams of his flannel.

He tried to scream, a raw, human sound of pure agony, but it broke halfway through, strangled by the sickening grind of shifting cartilage. 

I couldn't look away. My fingernails dug into my own palms as I watched his shoulders violently dislocate, dropping lower and resetting with a dull, meaty thud. His skin stretched drum-tight over muscles that coiled and swelled beneath the surface, rippling wildly as if things were burrowing underneath it. In the pale light, his flesh looked translucent, bruised purple and webbed with dark veins straining at the sudden expansion. 

He pitched forward onto all fours, his fingers digging trenches into the frozen dirt. I watched in horror as the bones in his hands snapped and lengthened, the joints swelling and splitting the skin at the knuckles before thick, hooked claws pushed out from ruined nail beds. Coarse, bristling black hair erupted across his forearms and shoulders in sudden, creeping waves, swallowing the stretched, glistening skin.

The worst of it was his face. 

He threw his head back, his jaw unhinging with a wet *pop* that made my stomach violently lurch. The bones of his skull seemed to liquefy and harden all at once, grinding together like millstones as the bridge of his nose and his jawline pushed outward, stretching the skin of his cheeks until his lips pulled permanently back from elongating, yellow-white teeth. His legs spasmed behind him; his shins bowed, his ankles cracking and shooting upward, lifting his heels permanently off the earth into the coiled haunches of a predator.

The ragged, pleading whimpers died in his ruined throat, replaced by a deep, vibrating rattle that seemed to shake the dead leaves around my boots.

Silence fell over the clearing again, broken only by the heavy, wet panting of lungs twice the size they had been two minutes ago. Steam billowed from a dark, blood-flecked muzzle. 

Slowly, the massive creature rose, towering even on crooked hind legs, shreds of flannel hanging uselessly from broad, matted shoulders. It shook itself once, the sound of damp fur slapping muscle echoing in the dark. 

Then, its ears twitched. The long, lupine head lifted, nostrils flaring wide as it drank in the cold night air—drinking in the scent of sweat, mud, and the terrified, racing pulse of prey. 

Glowing, amber eyes snapped directly toward the fallen oak. Directly at me.

In the dim, gas-lit basin of the 1840s operating theater, the air smelled thickly of sawdust, sweat, and old copper. Tiered wooden benches rose steeply around the central wooden table, packed with medical students leaning forward in hushed, morbid anticipation. There was no ether here, no chloroform—only leather straps, a bottle of brandy, and the terrifying necessity of speed. 

At the center stood the surgeon, wearing a stiff, black frock coat encrusted with the dried, darkened blood of dozens of previous operations—a badge of his experience. Beside him, a terrified laborer lay pinned to the table by four burly orderlies. The patient’s shattered leg hung over the edge above a bucket of fresh sawdust. A leather bit was forced between his teeth, though everyone in the room knew it wouldn't hold for long.

The surgeon picked up a long, narrow Liston knife, testing its balance for a fraction of a second. He looked up at the gallery, pocket watch in an assistant's hand. 

"Time me, gentlemen," the surgeon said calmly.

With terrifying velocity, the surgeon dropped into a slight crouch and swept the blade in a single, circular motion around the patient’s thigh. Skin and muscle parted instantly down to the bone. 

The leather bit popped from the patient’s mouth, followed by a sound that seemed to rattle the glass skylight above—a raw, guttural shriek of absolute agony that tore through the theater. The man arched his back violently, veins bulging in his neck, fighting against the crushing weight of the four orderlies holding his shoulders and hips.

Before the scream had even peaked, the blood came. Despite the heavy brass tourniquet screwed tight into the groin, dark venous blood welled up in a thick tide, while a smaller, missed collateral artery hissed, sending a bright crimson spray across the surgeon’s waistcoat, splashing onto his cuffs and spattering the boots of the nearest assistant. The sawdust beneath the table instantly turned black-red.

The surgeon did not flinch, blink, or pause to wipe his face. Speed was the only mercy he had to offer; every second lingered meant fatal shock. 

An assistant yanked the sliced skin and muscle upward with a linen retractor. Dropping the bloody knife to the floor—there was no time to set it down neatly—the surgeon snatched up a heavy bone saw. 

*Rasping, wet, and rhythmic.* Six, seven, eight furious strokes. Bone dust mingled with the pooling blood as the saw chewed through the femur. The patient’s screams dissolved into frantic, hyperventilating sobs, his eyes rolling back into his head, slick with cold sweat as the sheer trauma overloaded his senses. 

With a sharp crack, the limb separated and dropped heavily into the waiting hands of an assistant. 

Twenty-eight seconds had elapsed. 

Now came the frantic aftermath. The surgeon grabbed a tenaculum—a sharp, hooked instrument—and plunged it into the raw, quivering stump to fish out the severed femoral artery, clamping his teeth onto a silk ligature to keep his hands free while an assistant tied off the spurting vessels. As the tourniquet was slightly loosened to check for hidden bleeders, fresh jets of blood pulsed out, quickly caught and strangled with silk threads, their ends left dangling out of the wound.

Two heavy flaps of flesh were pulled down over the jagged bone and stitched shut with thick needles, eliciting one final, weak groan from the semi-conscious patient before he finally mercifully fainted. 

Silence fell back over the gallery, broken only by the ragged breathing of the orderlies and the rhythmic drip of crimson hitting the saturated sawdust below. The surgeon straightened up, wiped his dripping hands on a coarse towel, and bowed slightly to the applause of the students above.

The lantern between them was running out of oil, its stuttering amber flame casting long, frantic shadows against the cinderblock walls of the cellar. Outside, the relentless autumn rain drummed against the boarded-up bulkhead, a dull, rhythmic static that usually helped them sleep. Tonight, it just sounded like a countdown.

Julian sat slumped against a rusted shelving unit, a makeshift tourniquet knotted uselessly above his collarbone. Beneath the frayed collar of his flannel shirt, dark, spiderwebbed veins were already creeping upward toward his jaw. His skin had taken on the translucent, waxy pallor of old candle tallow. Every breath he pulled into his lungs rattled like dry leaves.

"It could just be an infection," Marcus whispered. He was pacing the narrow concrete floor, his boots scraping through years of dust. He kept wiping his palms on his jeans, unable to look at Julian for more than a second at a time. "A regular one. Sepsis. Those things have rotting teeth, right? We still have that amoxicillin from the vet clinic in Oakhaven. Clara, tell him. Tell him we have the pills."

Clara didn't look up from the heavy revolver resting across her knees. Her thumbs traced the worn checkered grip, over and over, feeling the minuscule grooves filled with dried mud and old sweat. 

"The pills won't touch this, Marc," Clara said. Her voice sounded hollowed out, scraped raw by smoke and three years of burying people she loved. "You see his eyes."

Julian’s irises, normally a sharp, startling blue, were clouding at the edges, bleeding into a milky gray. He shivered violently, his teeth clacking together so hard Clara worried they might shatter. 

"I'm cold," Julian rasped. He tried to smile, to offer the same easygoing deflection he’d used when they ran out of food in January, or when their truck threw a rod fifty miles from nowhere. Instead, his face twisted in a sudden spasm of agony. He gripped his knees, knuckles white, until the wave passed. When he looked up again, tears were cutting clean tracks through the grime on his cheeks. "God, Clara. I can feel it behind my eyes. It’s like static. Like I’m losing the station."

Marcus stopped pacing. A choked sound escaped his throat, and he dropped to his knees beside Julian, grabbing his uninjured shoulder. "Don't talk like that. You're just burning up. We’ll cool you down. We’ll get wet rags—"

"Marc, stop," Julian breathed, leaning his feverish forehead against Marcus's wrist. "Please. Don't make me wake up hungry. Don't let me look at you two and not know who you are."

The silence that followed was suffocating. It pressed down on them, heavier than the concrete ceiling above. 

Clara slowly stood up. Her joints ached; everything ached. The revolver felt impossibly heavy in her right hand, dragging her arm down toward the floor as if gravity itself was protesting what came next. She looked at Julian—the man who had taught her how to hotwire a sedan, who knew the names of every constellation left in the unpolluted sky, who always saved the sweetened condensed milk from ration packs for her birthday. 

Once she pulled the trigger, all of that would evaporate. There was no going back from it. In the old world, death was sanitized, tucked behind hospital curtains and softened by machines that beeped gently until they didn't. Here, death was violent, loud, and absolute. She had to be the one to sever the thread, to turn a living, breathing friend with a voice and a history into quiet, cooling weight. 

"I can't watch," Marcus sobbed, burying his face in Julian’s damp jacket, clutching at the fabric like a child. "I can't do this again. Not Julian. Please, Clara, give him another hour. Just one more hour."

"In an hour, it won't be me you're giving it to," Julian whispered. His gaze drifted past Marcus, locking onto Clara. The gray was swallowing the blue rapidly now. His breathing hitched, turning shallow and erratic. Terror—pure, lucid terror—flashed across his features as a muscle in his neck twitched involuntarily. "Clara. Now. While I still remember your name. Say my name, and do it."

Clara stepped forward until the toes of her boots touchedJulian’s outstretched legs. Her hands were shaking so violently the cylinder of the revolver rattled faintly in its housing. She raised the weapon with both hands, bracing her wrists, yet the front sight danced wildly in the dying lantern light. 

"Look at the wall, Marc," Clara said, her voice breaking cleanly in half. "Cover your ears."

Marcus didn't move, only wept harder, holding tight to Julian's arm, grounding him to the earth for the last few seconds he belonged to it.

Julian closed his eyes and tilted his chin up slightly, an act of profound, devastating trust that nearly brought Clara to her knees. His lips moved, soundlessly forming words—a prayer, a memory, an apology—before his jaw clenched tight against another tremor.

"Julian," Clara whispered, tears blinding her, turning the cellar into a blur of shadow and amber light. "I'm so sorry, Jules."

She pulled the hammer back. The sharp metallic *click* echoed through the small room like a bone snapping. 

For one agonizing heartbeat, she hovered on the precipice, desperate for a miracle, for the universe to intervene and stay her hand. None came. Only the rain outside, indifferent and endless.

She squeezed the trigger.

The roar of the gunshot was deafening in the confined space, a violent flash of white light that slammed against their eardrums and sucked all the air out of the room. The smell of burnt cordite instantly overwhelmed the damp earthiness of the cellar. 

Then, the ringing faded, replaced by a silence far worse than the one before. 

The lantern finally guttered out, plunging them into the dark. Marcus let out a long, ragged wail that tore through the pitch black, rocking back and forth beside the sudden, irreversible absence of their friend. Clara let the revolver slip from her numb fingers. It clattered onto the concrete, empty of purpose, leaving her standing alone in the dark with the ringing in her ears and the unbearable weight of having survived.
